messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi Mensah is a fifty-year-old Ghanaian-American plumber, married for twenty-two years, who was referred for psychological assessment following a violent assault that occurred approximately eight months ago. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 73, indicating severe posttraumatic symptomatology, and describes a clinical picture that has progressively narrowed his world to the point where his wife has issued what she calls a quiet ultimatum: get help, or she does not know how much longer she can watch him disappear.

The assault took place on an evening when Kofi had stayed late to finish a commercial job in an unfamiliar part of the city. As he was loading tools into his van in a poorly lit parking structure, two men approached from his peripheral vision and attacked him without warning. One struck him from the side before he could register the movement, and what followed was a sustained and brutal beating during which Kofi was unable to defend himself or call for help. He lay on the concrete for some time before a passerby found him. He sustained a fractured orbital socket, cracked ribs, and a concussion. No arrests were ever made.

What Kofi carries from that night is not a story he can tell so much as a set of images he cannot stop seeing — the angle of the fluorescent light above him, the texture of the concrete against his cheek, the shadows of the men's legs. He has found, to his distress, that he cannot seem to put the event into words in any coherent way. When asked to describe what happened, he goes quiet and his eyes move as though watching something play out just above the interviewer's shoulder. The memories come as pictures, vivid and unbidden, and with them arrives an overwhelming sense of guilt — a conviction, not entirely rational but deeply felt, that he should have done something, that a man of his experience and physicality should not have ended up on that floor. This guilt, bound tightly to the images themselves, has come to colour how he understands the attack: not as something that was done to him, but as evidence of something already lacking in him. These memory intrusions and the guilt they carry feed directly into a state of near-constant vigilance, as though his nervous system has concluded that the world that produced that night is still present and watching. Any unexpected movement nearby — a colleague rounding a corner on a job site, a customer's dog darting across a hallway — produces a full-body startle response that embarrasses and frightens him in equal measure.

Kofi has come to believe that he is no longer the man he was. For over two decades he has taken pride in being the kind of tradesman who could work anywhere, in any conditions, alone or alongside strangers. That identity has been dismantled. He now feels safe only in a very limited number of places — primarily his own home, and occasionally his brother-in-law's house nearby. He will not take jobs that require working alone in enclosed or unfamiliar spaces, which in his trade is nearly every job. His employer has noticed. Kofi is aware that this is costing him professionally and financially, but what frightens him most is the conviction that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing if something were to happen again — that some essential competence or courage has been permanently removed. This appraisal of himself as diminished and unreliable sustains the hypervigilance rather than easing it, because a man who cannot trust himself must be watched over by himself constantly. The threat feels everywhere because he has decided, somewhere beneath conscious reflection, that the protection he once assumed he could provide is gone.

The hypervigilance has its own cost in the night hours. Kofi sleeps poorly, waking at sounds or movements, and arrives at each morning already exhausted. In that state, the intrusive images return more easily, and the cycle — memory sharpening threat, threat dragging memory back — has become the texture of his daily life. He has not spoken to his wife about the guilt. What finally brought him to the clinic was her telling him, gently but plainly, that she missed him. What he is most afraid of is that she is right — that the person she misses no longer exists.
